No stretch longer than about 20 s of narration should run over a still canvas; the 80-s overnight repo story needs its own scene (report deadline, short cash, overnight loan, repayment).
A worked example that promises a calculation (4% for one day) must finish it with the actual figure on screen.
Opposite mechanisms should reuse the same diagram mirrored, with only the direction and one word changed (worked here for reverse repo).
A policy effect taught by a state swap (decreased to increased on the same diagram) is a reusable pattern for two-direction cause and effect.
Labels that rename a rate ('rate of discount') must be checked against the book; flag terms the source does not use.
Reasons that sound like rule-dodging (borrow overnight to show a clean CRR/SLR report) must be checked and worded neutrally.
The closing recap should restate the links between terms, not only list their names.
A good/bad verdict about a term must put a visible mark on that term's own picture; flag more than about 20 s of speech over an unchanged frame.
When a spoken example uses numbers (7% to 4%), those numbers should be labelled on the picture they describe.
A stretch of real data labelled with a term must match the shape rule taught for it (disinflation = still rising, only slower); a flat stretch should not carry that label without saying why.
A policy cure (reflation) should be drawn as tools acting on the same curve, not as a caption sentence read aloud.
The colour given to each term must stay the same across the made-up chart and the real chart (worked well here; enforce it).
Branches of a tree should be drawn in the order the narration names them (unemployment was named before NPAs).
The closing recap should be spoken over the finished pictures, not the end card.
A worked formula result must agree with the running example it reuses (12,100 / 10 = 1,210 while the peel-back story landed on 10,000); a numeric consistency check should catch it.
When an index such as a deflator is used, its scale (base = 100) must be stated with the number.
Every derived cell in a table should be reached by an arrow from its source cell (done here; enforce).
When a term is transformed into another (nominal into real), strike the old word and write the new one at the moment the voice says it (done here; enforce).
Reasons given only as text cards for more than about 20 s (the 2015 switch) should be flagged for a picture.
BIE must not show real organisation emblems (UN flag) or invent viewer names for shout-outs.
Keep the varying quantity to one: holding output at 1 while price changes isolated the idea cleanly; a check can require one variable changing per numeric example.
A term defined as a pattern of steps (recession = two contractions in a row) must be drawn as one band spanning exactly those steps on the same chart.
The agenda should list terms in the order they will be taught.
The recap must be spoken over the finished chart, not over the end card.
The defining words must match the slope on screen: a GDP fall must not be called a 'declining growth rate' when the same video teaches slower growth as a separate idea.
Axis and unit setup before the first term should stay under about 20 s or state why it matters.
A spoken number change (6% to 7-8%) about a chart piece should get a label on that piece.
Every number on screen must be spoken (60 and 55 appear only on screen).
A number should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice reaches it (65 leads by about 9 s).
When the voice says something is unchanged (demand, supply in cost-push), the screen should mark it unchanged; E15 does this only for the bottleneck case.
Comparing causes should reuse one scene and mark only the node that changed (E15 does this; enforce it).
A stretch of more than about 60 s with only text boxes (the Monetarist view) should be flagged for a picture.
A transcript where one token repeats many times is a failed transcript: re-run with language detection before any timing check (E15's narration was English, forced Hindi produced loops).
If a case is named as a subtype of two things (bottleneck from a supply drop, yet 'still demand-pull'), the lesson must say plainly how both hold.

A real case with two numbers to compare (above 20% vs below 11%) needs a picture of the comparison (for example two bars); flag a canvas that stays unchanged for more than about 30 s while a case is told.
When the voice says some items fall, at least one item on screen must show a down arrow.
No promo overlay may cover the canvas while a teaching sentence is being spoken.
Term nodes that pop in about 0.5-1.5 s before the spoken term work well; flag nodes more than 3 s early, or after the word.
A definition box that repeats the voice word for word should be replaced by the visual it describes or cut.
Every percentage written on screen (4.5%, 18%, 77.5%) must be spoken, or labelled as 'current value' with its date.
Two different values for the same quantity in one video (gap 'back to 1%', then 'today 0.25%') must be caught by a consistency check and resolved in the script.
When a worked number example runs, each derived number must land on the arrow or actor it belongs to (done here; enforce).
A rule given as a written formula (repo + penalty = MSF) should be followed by the same rule in numbers (6.5 + 0.25 = 6.75) on the same screen.
Imported real-data charts must be redrawn from data, and any line the voice does not name (reverse repo) removed or named.
A new mechanism laid over an old one gets its own colour, and the old channel fades when the new rule is explained (worked here).
BIE's own narration audio should be re-transcribed and matched to the script; a stretch over 10 s with no recognised words flags a dropped or garbled line (this video's transcript lost about 50 s).
A threshold in a definition (10% stake) should be drawn as a quantity against a marked line, not only written; the same for a stated stake (77%).
A cause_effect list (benefits of FDI) shown as text bullets should be flagged; each cause needs a picture of the step (goods crossing a customs gate vs made inside).
Every acronym must be unpacked at first mention (E18 does this for all six; enforce it).
A long sub-branch (more than about 90 s) should end with a recap on the anchor picture before the next branch (E18 does this at 130 s; enforce it).
The second side of a contrast (QFI 'fewer regulations') should not appear on screen before the voice has finished the first side.
When the voice names two names for one thing (RFPI officially, FPI in the news), the screen should show both, linked.
A term named in the closing (offshore derivative instrument) must get at least a one-line yaani unpack, even if the detail is deferred.
Real brand logos and real takeover names should be replaced by generic companies in BIE's own lessons.
Questions promised in the agenda (depreciation vs devaluation, who does it) must be answered in the lesson or explicitly deferred; flag open promises at the end.
Every number on screen must be spoken (±1% is on screen; the voice says 'some percent').
Every effect named on screen must be spoken (balance of payment crisis is only on screen).
The agent on screen must match the agent in the voice (screen: government devalued; voice: central bank devalues).
After a rule change (devaluation), re-run the same running example with the new number (E19 does this with the car; enforce it).
A definition note should not appear more than about 3 s before its term (the hard-peg note leads by about 6 s).
No caricatures of real people or brand founders; BIE uses its own recurring characters.
A humour beat must not replace the bridge question's teaching; the question should still be spoken and pictured.
A question put to the viewer (arithmetic vs geometric mean) must be answered later in the same video, or the script fails.
Every number shown on screen must be spoken or labelled as reference: here 20 Rs, the chair's 193.77 and the 2022-23 monthly values were shown but never said.

When a story sets numbers (1000 then, 5000 now) and a formula comes later (current / base x 100), the formula must be applied to the story's numbers once (index 500 vs rise 400%); here that link was missed.
A data table on screen shows only the rows the narration names; a 22-row weight table held for 44 s with one value spoken should be collapsed or stepped through.
Named formulas and proper nouns (Laspeyres, Jevons, DPIIT) need a pronunciation entry for BIE's voice and subtitles taken from the script, since recognition garbled them here.
A running example started on one item (the chair) must be carried into the aggregate step on screen (done here with one line from I1 to W1); enforce for every worked calculation.
Time-bound remarks ('we are in December 2022', months not yet available) must carry a date stamp or be removed.
Claims flagged for fact review against the source book: WPI for macro vs CPI for micro policy, and 'point-to-point' explained as comparison with the same month of the base year.
Idle decorative animation (a waving flag) must stop while teaching changes happen; 4 of 24 change points here were only the flag.
Absolute claims ('100% nationalised', 'all industries') must be flagged for a fact check before narration; the card notes this one is not accurate.
When a count carries the point (14 banks, 85% of business, 7 associates), draw that many items or a filling share, not only a text note.
A text-only screen held for more than about 20 s with no drawn actor should be flagged (private-bank paragraph, before/after boxes).
In a history video every law or committee should have a spoken cause before it and a spoken effect after it (this video mostly does; enforce).
History videos should end by clearing to the bare timeline as a recap (done here; enforce).
Same-name items (Committee I and II) must have the reason for the numbering spoken (done here; enforce).
Constant decorative motion (the spinning globe) must stop during teaching beats; it hid two minutes of changes from the change detector and competes with the step being taught.
A list of dealings that each move money in or out should be drawn as flows into or out of the reserve, with direction, not as a bullet list.
A 'yaad rakhiye' rule that splits one thing two ways (principal vs interest) must show both halves on screen; only the interest half was drawn.
A topic built on plus/minus balances needs at least one small worked number example; this video has none.
Every short form shown on screen (BoT, NFIA, CAS, CAD) must be expanded by the voice at first use (done here; enforce).
A definition side note (BoP crisis) should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice reaches the term, and promo banners must not cover the canvas while the final definition is spoken.
More than about 8 new terms per minute in a classification tree should trigger a split into two scenes or a recap.

Every date, 'first' and 'only' in a history script must be checked against the book source before narration (here: Madras and Bombay years look swapped; 'world's only privately owned central bank' and 'Britain's central bank was government-owned' are doubtful for 1935; agency houses described as Indian lalas and seths).
The opening hook must not contradict the body (the hook says PNB and Allahabad Bank began under the British; the body calls them private joint-stock banks, PNB with Lala Lajpat Rai).
A spoken cause chain with actors and actions (panic, withdrawals, banks failing) must get a picture in the scene plan, not only a note; flag 'chain with no picture'.
A merger must be shown as the merging things joining (three buildings sliding into one), never only as a text note.
A timeline object must not appear more than about 3 s before the narration reaches it (three buildings appeared about 11 s early).
When a story derives a concept ('agency houses are now working like banks'), the scene plan should relabel the same actor at that conclusion line (worked here).
On-screen notes must pass a spelling and grammar check ('Presidency Houses' for presidency banks; 'owned entirely was private shareholders').
Emotive national framing in history ('why did the British do this to us') must be flagged for neutral wording.
A history video with more than about 15 dates should end with a spoken and drawn timeline recap.
Present-day bank logos used as examples should be replaced by generic buildings with name labels.
Numbers that carry the punchline (here 10%, 9%, 8.3%) must be spoken or pointed at by the voice, not only appear on screen.
The term being defined must be named while its diagram is still on screen; no promo or end card may start before the term and its conclusion line are finished.
When a formula is read aloud, highlight each table cell as it is used and substitute real numbers at least once.
Flag any table that stays unchanged for more than about 20 s while the narration moves on.
In a cause-effect concept the cause must be said in one plain line (the same rise on a bigger base gives a smaller %), not left for the viewer to work out.

In a role-play opening, the term is named only after the scene ends, and the later explanation of failure must point back to a moment of the scene (here the rival-bank offer becomes the competition reason).
When a number in a running example is revised, the old value stays visible and struck, so the history of the change can be read.
Every item of an on-screen list must be spoken (three of the four base-rate inputs are never said).
A text answer must not appear more than about 3 s before the voice gives it (the 'because banks were competing' line leads by about 6 s).
Key evidence numbers (77% of lending below the floor) must be drawn as a quantity against the floor line, not only written.
Goals planted as on-screen chips must be resolved on the same chips (cross on failure, tick on success); E25 does this well.
Statements about who decides (RBI fixed BPLR vs BPLR settled with banks) must stay consistent within one lesson; flag contradictions between narration lines.
When two successive systems are compared, reuse one scene and change only the parts that differ (tag, ring, arrow direction).
A spoken analogy must get a picture in the scene plan; here the strongest idea (inner-pocket cash on a bus) has none.
Content promised 'in this video' (CAR, CRAR, RWA, tier capital) must be delivered or explicitly moved to the next video before the end.
Spoken years and numbers must match on-screen text (Basel 1: transcript 1998, screen 1988); a check should compare them and flag for audio review.
Abbreviation-to-full-name lines with no idea drawn (CAR, CRAR, RWA) should be flagged as names without meaning.
A consequence chain (failure, contagion, credit crunch, downturn) must be drawn as a chain, not as bullets.
'Prices fluctuate' needs a moving price line; a list of asset names does not show market risk.
A sidebar chapter map that lights the current part worked; enforce it for overview-then-details videos.
Every input of a spoken result must be spoken or shown at the same moment: a yield of 10% needs its price (5,000) said, not only placed on a later graph.
Every computed percentage in the script must match its arithmetic and one rounding rule (500/9,000 = 5.56%, shown as 5.5%).
A story the narrator tells about a name (golden edges on British bonds) must get a picture in the scene plan; flag 'story with no picture'.
Real bank and company names and logos as characters must be replaced by generic actors (Bank A, Company B).
A teaser line ('important concept in the next 2 minutes') must name the concept, and the scene that pays it off must follow within the stated time.
When two terms differ on one yes/no property (sold at a discount?), the scene plan should use a yes/no fork (worked well here).
Definitions that narrow or redefine a standard term (G-sec only for non-discounted bonds; yield as interest in the secondary market) must be checked against the book source and flagged.
On-screen definition paragraphs over about 25 words should be split into labelled steps or replaced by the picture of the process.
A taxonomy of more than about 8 nodes before the first example should be cut to the path the lesson takes; the rest shown only as a road map.
A promo overlay must never cover a recap screen.
When the narration names a transfer between parties (risk moves from A to B), the scene must move one object from A to B; a text label alone fails.
A conditional rule (if X defaults, B pays A) needs the trigger event and the payout drawn as steps (a default mark on the bond, a money arrow from B to A), not only a paragraph.
On-screen rule text must not appear more than about 3 s before the voice starts saying it.
Idle character loops count as decoration: flag a scene where more than a third of the visual changes carry no meaning.
A pain named in the hook must be visibly resolved when the concept solves it (awake to asleep), before the end card.
A 'regular' or 'periodic' payment must be animated as at least two repeated pulses.
A worked example must obey the limits of the instrument it illustrates: the T-bill example used a 2-year security while T-bills run 364 days at most.
Every step the narration gives a mechanism must be drawn: the repo buy-back (securities returning, cash plus interest going back) and term money were spoken but never shown.
An exception that contradicts a definition given earlier (CDs by AIFIs for 1-3 years still called money market instruments, though money market means up to 364 days) must be reconciled in the script.
Sibling concepts reuse one picture template (here: issuer, security down, cash up, name bar, limits callout for T-bill, CD and CP); BIE's scene plan should enforce one template per family.
No scene may sit unchanged for more than about 30 s while new terms or limits are spoken (participants strip about 140 s, CD about 60 s).
Real brand logos (a named bank) and real state emblems must be replaced with generic icons.
Speech-gap detection must use word start times: a 12 s loss inside one segment (763.7-776.0 s) was invisible to segment-end checks.
A one-line 'seen from the other side it is X' (repo vs reverse repo) needs its own picture and a check against the source book, since the term has a narrower policy meaning in India.
A running money example must balance: parts sum to the whole (75 + 18 + 4 + 3 = 100 lakh) and the tally equals its rows (7.5 + 1.08 - 3 - 5 = 0.58 lakh); worked here, enforce in code.
Number checks that compare transcript and screen must understand Hindi 'each' doubling ('teen-teen lakh' heard as '33 lakh'), so a false alarm is not raised and a real mismatch is not missed.
A worked example must say whether members' money is a deposit (earns interest) or share capital (earns dividend); here the same 1 crore is treated as both.
Leftover cash and yearly expenses are different things; 'the remaining 3 lakh is spent on expenses' should be flagged as a stock-flow mix-up.
Structural claims (UCBs under DCCBs, UCBs serving PCS) must be checked against the book source.
Regulatory facts must carry an 'as of' date (the 2020 Banking Regulation amendment changed RBI's powers over co-op banks); 'NABARD regulates' should read 'supervises/inspects' if the book says so.
Real bank logos used as characters must be replaced by generic bank marks.
A list with a moving highlight should not hold one canvas for over about 30 s; each item gets a small scene or the list is cut.
One colour per entity type kept through the whole video (worked here: yellow PCS, orange UCB, dark green DCCB, light green state bank); enforce as a scene check.
A table of results should reveal row by row as each row is spoken, not all at once 5-20 s early.
A worked example must be named in the narration: here the egg, its index 150.40 and its weight 0.36 appear only on screen; every number the calculation lands on must be spoken.

A question to the viewer must get a real answer: the WPI video's open question (why the geometric mean) is answered here only as 'international practice'; BIE should give the reason (an outlier quote pulls an arithmetic mean more).

When two videos teach the same method (WPI and CPI calculation), BIE should reuse the same scene template and say so ('the same steps as WPI'), and keep the formula names and pronunciations identical.

Claims flagged for fact review against the source book: which bureau compiles CPI-UNME, the example jobs for industrial workers (IT sector), the foreign-company DA use of CPI-UNME, and the start year of CPI rural/urban/combined.
No real-person photo, brand pack or stray mouse cursor may appear in a BIE scene; replace with generic icons and clean renders.
A table of many numbers (18 weights) must be read as a comparison: show only the cells the narration discusses, or turn the columns into bars.
A rule stated as text tags (MMRP, 'partial index') needs its own picture: for MMRP, three windows of different length on a calendar.

A sentence repeated by an editing slip (the calculation start said twice) should be caught by a script check for near-duplicate consecutive lines; about 31 s of garbled or missing speech should be flagged by word-start gap and repetition checks.
Legal sources named in a script must be checked against the book (here both ratios are tagged 'RBI Act 1949'; CRR is usually under the RBI Act 1934 and SLR under the Banking Regulation Act 1949).
Every 'current value' (CRR 4.5%, SLR 18%) must carry its date and be compared with the run date; stale values are flagged.
Eligibility lists (which assets count as SLR securities) must be verified against the source before narration; this list looks wrong.
A recap table should not be rebuilt cell by cell right after the same rules were taught (about 100 s here); reveal it whole as a summary.
Lists of more than about 4 items should become a sort-into-groups scene or icons, not lines of text written one by one.
A policy effect (what changing the ratio does) must get its own scene: the dial moves and the lendable arrow shrinks or grows.
An open-loop question ('for now take the answer as no') must be closed later in the same script; pair them in a check (done here at 415 s).
Framing check: 'RBI wants to raise inflation' should read 'RBI accepts some inflation to support growth'.
Re-transcribe BIE's narration; a gap of more than 10 s without words (508-522 s here) flags a dropped line.
Spoken time words ('today', 'aaj ki rate') must agree with the date on screen; flag a 'today' claim shown with an older dated note.
Screenshots of real sources with unreadable text should be redrawn as BIE's own simple table holding only the rows the narration uses.
Every big number should carry a unit and a scale anchor (months of imports, times since a year); this video does it and it should be a rule.
Content on screen at the start (the four-part sum) must be spoken or marked as recall within about 5 s.
Voice timing must be word level and complete; a recognition gap over about 5 s blocks talmel checks and should fail the voice stage.
Counts said must match lists shown (10 small banks said; the table shows more rows).
Dates on screen must match the narration (wallets 'from 2006' in voice, 'before 2013' on screen).
No real person photos or quotes as decoration; cite the source in text only.
Every 'not allowed' rule should be shown as a struck item or a blocked arrow (E34 does both; enforce it).
A reasons list held as text for more than about 40 s should be flagged; each reason needs its own small picture.
Elements with no stated meaning (the row of thin up-arrows) should be flagged as decoration.
Superlative claims ('first in the world') must be marked for fact-checking before reuse.
Reusing the opening problem picture for a later idea (the crowd box for wallets) should be encouraged, so the learner compares slices.
Made-up country figures must carry an on-screen 'example, not reality' note while they are shown (E35 does this; enforce it everywhere).
Every number shown on screen (138 crore) should be spoken, or dropped.
An actor the picture adds (the government as spender) must also be named by the voice.
When the voice rejects a definition, the screen must visibly strike it (the red cross on the growth title worked; enforce it).
A derived value (per capita = GDP / population) should show its division step on screen, not only the results.
Notes that repeat the narration should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice reaches them.
A cliff-hanger close must still recap what was settled before opening the next question.
Superlative claims ('first and only fully private central bank in the world') and who-did-what claims (who bought the 92% stake) must be flagged for a fact check before narration.
When an on-screen reason differs from the spoken reason (public trust), the scene check should flag the mismatch.
History narration should keep timeline order, or mark a flashback on screen; here the 1937 move is told after 1947.
Names shown on screen but not spoken (eight associate banks) should be either read or placed on a map, not left as a list.
Idle flag animation produced 2 of 24 change points; decorative motion must pause during teaching beats.
Series continuity: open on the previous video's last canvas and end on the canvas the next one opens with (done here; worth keeping as a rule for multi-part topics).
Every law on a history timeline should have its question or cause spoken before it (done here; enforce).
Spoken option letters in an elimination must match the options crossed on screen (here 'A, C and D' was said while a, b, d were crossed): a script-vs-scene check.
Every numeric question needs its working drawn on screen (formula, then numbers, then result); Q5 showed only a tick after 30 s of still page.
Every figure given in a question that the solution does not use must be named as a distractor with the reason (the 10,000 non-debt receipts in Q5).

Generated practice: each false statement must differ from a true fact in exactly one checkable element (number, category, actor or an extreme word), and must carry a link to the lesson node that refutes it.

When the answer is reached by elimination, the narration must say which statements no longer need checking and why, and one surviving statement should be confirmed positively (Q6 did the confirmation but not the explanation).
An evidence scene must restate its fact in the narration; text that only sits on screen (the bovine definition, census numbers, vertical and horizontal) does not count as taught.
BIE must not reuse lessons as filmed screens with small text; an evidence scene is re-rendered on the canvas, with the lesson's own narration line included in the script and subtitles.

Speech recognition lost about 245 s here, mostly replayed lesson audio: when BIE builds a practice video from lesson clips, the clip lines must come from the script, not from re-recognition, and any 10 s window with no recognised words is flagged.

When the narration voices a learner's doubt and reasons it out (the gold-ETF price argument), the canvas must show at least one step of the reasoning; flag 'question mark only' stretches longer than 20 s.

A comparison of two products should show each difference as an action (a live ticker vs a once-a-day stamp, a big team vs one person), not only bullets; flag compare_two_sides segments with more than 60 on-screen words and no motion.
Flag spoken statements that contradict on-screen text (spoken 'MF units only after market close' vs screen 'priced at end-of-day NAV').
Category claims must be checked: 'X is a kind of Y' (REIT described as an ETF in real estate) should be flagged for verification.
Real-person photos and quotes must be replaced by a generic expert figure and a paraphrase.
A claim about cost (MF charges more) should come with one number or a visible cost token; flag cost comparisons with no number.
When sibling products share one mechanism, prefer reusing the same scene template and swapping only the changed part.
Transcript gaps over 10 s inside teaching must be re-transcribed before talmel scoring (13-30 s, 230-244 s, 278-291 s here).

A spoken story longer than about 20 s with two or more actors and a transfer (A sells to B, NBFC pays A, NBFC collects from B) must have those actors and transfers drawn; a still canvas during such a story fails.
An on-screen list of N items where the voice covers fewer (nine exempt types, three spoken) must be cut to what is spoken, or every item must be spoken.
Real brand names (banks, broking apps) in examples are replaced by generic names before rendering.
Internal consistency: an entity shown as exempt from a regulator (housing finance companies) must not also appear as one of that regulator's categories without a line explaining the change.
Regulatory facts that changed over time (who regulates HFCs; the current list of NBFC types) need a dated source check before use.
A full form shown on screen (Infrastructure Debt Fund) must be spoken, or the code alone shown.
Definitions are checked against an authoritative glossary; a description that contradicts the usual definition (CIC-SI as 'investment in core sectors') blocks the scene.

When the voice asks the learner's question, a '?' is placed on the item in question and replaced by the answer when it is given (worked here at 144-163 s); enforce this pattern for every voiced objection.
A transcript gap over 10 s inside a run flags a dropped or garbled narration line (here about 75.5-90 s).
Normalise Indian number words (lakh, crore) before comparing transcript numbers with on-screen numbers: '5 lakh' came out as 5,000,000.
A figure the voice compares against (1.25 crore) must be on screen next to the figure it is compared with (11 crore).
An arrow must point from the actor to the target the narration names: banks register with Mudra, so the 'Registered' arrow points to Mudra.
When the voice says 'the calculation can be seen here', every step of the sum must be on screen (1 lakh + 10K - 5K = 1.05 lakh).
Spell-check on-screen headings ('BENEFIARY').
A problem sentence in the script (no loans, moneylenders, cannot grow) must get its own picture before the solution appears.
Institution names and status should go to a fact check (MUDRA is usually described as a SIDBI subsidiary, not a bank; the interest rule may be outdated).
No real logos, emblems or photos of real people; replace with generic drawings.
A transcript word whose end time lies more than 5 s after its start hides a gap (274.9-291.6 s here); flag it.
Numbers should not appear more than about 2 s before they are spoken (here up to 10 s early).
No still stretch longer than about 45 s while the narration adds new reasons or examples: every spoken reason (purpose, two stories, risk-return at 142-236 s) needs its own on-screen change.
Every item in a spoken list must be drawn and every drawn item spoken: insurance (said, not drawn), dividend (drawn, not heard), Ministry of Consumer Affairs (said, not drawn).
A written reason must match the spoken reason at the same moment ('operating since ancient and medieval times' on screen vs 'stronger connections' in speech).
A boundary should be written and spoken in one form (screen 'up to 364 / more than 364 days', speech '364 or less / 365 or more').
Real brand logos and bank names used as examples must be swapped for a generic bank icon before rendering.
No promotional overlay may cover the teaching area while a teaching change is happening (518-536 s hides the 'belongs to unorganised' line).
Transcript QA: flag any single word lasting more than about 5 s as a hidden gap and re-transcribe that window before talmel or sync checks.
Factual check list for this topic: legal status of chit funds, nidhi companies and money lenders (state chit-fund and money-lender laws, company law) before saying 'no regulator'.

Screen labels must agree with the narration on direction words: the inflow list says 'import of goods' where the voice says export; a code check can compare import/export, buy/sell, in/out between script and on-screen text.
Country-classification facts (which countries free float or manage) need a dated source before they go on screen; Canada and Japan are usually classified as free floating.
When a mechanism has been drawn as a picture (RBI selling from reserves at 361 s), a later question about the same mechanism should reuse that picture rather than switch to a text chain.
Exchange-rate direction words ('the rate falls' = rupee stronger) must come with the quote convention on screen (rupees per dollar).
A worked example with numbers should be carried into the new rule: here the Rs 3.3 lakh never changes, so 'demand raises the price' is never seen as a number.
Confusable term pairs (depreciation/devaluation) should get an explicit 'notice the word' moment and a 2 x 2 placement, as done here; enforce for other pairs.
No promo overlay may cover a definition while it is spoken (468-480 s).
Sentence boxes over about 25 words that stay on a still canvas for more than 30 s are flagged (66-128 s).
When a numeric table is shown, every number the learner should keep must be read or visibly pointed to; flag tables where shown numbers outnumber spoken ones by more than 5 to 1.

A named formula or method (Laspeyres, Paasche, weighted arithmetic mean) must appear on screen within about 2 s of being spoken, and should be shown working at least once; flag voice-only formula names.
Flag claims about which formula an official Indian index uses for fact-checking before reuse (here the food indices are said to use Laspeyres and Paasche).
Flag any stretch over 20 s with no canvas change while a new idea is being spoken (270-298 s here).

A sub-index built from a parent should be shown as selection from the parent (arrow from the parent's items into the child's basket, non-members struck); check that the child's elements visibly come from the parent.
The order of labels on screen must match the spoken order (screen R-C-U vs spoken rural-urban-combined).
An outcome claim (index swing passed to FCI, cheap grain for the vulnerable) needs its end shown (grain reaching people), not only the agency's logo.
A transcript gap over 5 s that covers a highlighted item (236-243 s) must be re-transcribed before talmel scoring.

Running-number ledger: every number shown must be spoken and every number spoken must be shown (private placement 10% and founder 40% shown only; 4 lakh and 80 crore spoken only; 'discounted price' written only).

Cap-table arithmetic check: after each new issue, all holders' shares must add to 100% and existing holders must dilute in proportion, unless the script says the founder is selling his own shares; flag a stage that takes the whole new stake from one holder.
Glossary check for instrument definitions before rendering (OFCD vs fully convertible, partly vs 'semi' convertible, rights issue price and who may buy).
Every deal in a funding story uses the same two-way template (capital in, equity or certificate out, holder's number struck and rewritten); a round drawn without one of the two flows is incomplete.
A key term spoken as the purpose of a stage (minimum viable product, the VC fund manager and pool) must get a picture or at least a label at that moment.
Real company or business-group names used as examples must be replaced with generic investors.
Transcript QA: when a transcript gap overlaps a visual change that reveals a new term (98 s, 464-473 s), re-transcribe that window before the talmel check.
Pace check: no more than about 5 new terms in any 90 s window for school levels (the debenture types pack about 8).

Every rule stated as fact must be checked against national-accounts conventions before reuse: unsold stock (change in inventories) and own-account production of goods are part of GDP, unlike what rule 3 says here.

Institution facts need a date and a source: the CSO was merged into the National Statistical Office in 2019 under the statistics ministry; ministry names and office-holders said aloud must be verified or left out.
Numbers on screen and in the transcript must agree (Shyam 2 lakh vs 2,000); a mismatch is either a recognition error to recheck or a script error.
A term must not appear on screen before it is taught (final goods in a caption at 180 s, taught at 364 s).
Transcript gaps over 10 s that cover a number on screen (packets, ₹400, ₹15) must be flagged and the line re-recorded or re-transcribed.
A question handed to the viewer (shopkeeper's margin) must be answered somewhere in the course; BIE should schedule the answer in the next lesson's recall or in the notes.
Lessons with several rules should show a visible step tracker and a growing rule list, as here; a check can require one for any lesson with more than three numbered points.
Measures named in the opening (NDP, GNP, NNP) but not taught should be marked 'next lesson' on screen, not left as live branches.
Real brands (spice maker, steel maker, software firms, insurer's website, resale site) are replaced with generic ones.
Every term in a formula (here subsidies) must get a number in the worked example at least once, or the script must say why it is zero.
Every number the narration computes (the shopkeeper's 12,000) should appear on the picture where it belongs.
On-screen labels must use the word being taught: a factor cost result must not be labelled 'price'.
A highlight must not jump to the opposite answer while the voice is still on the old one (Market Price lit while 'factor cost' is being said).
A single transcript word stretched over more than 5 s hides a gap (14.7-26.9 s here) and must be flagged like a missing stretch.
Real brand names on generic icons (a bank) must be replaced with a generic bank.
When the narration lists factor payments, a classification check should flag intermediate inputs (electricity, maintenance, raw material) put in the factor column.
The most exam-relevant point should not be left as a comment-box question; if the answer is deferred, the script must link it.

Check definitions against standard national accounts before reuse: NFIA is net factor income (compensation of employees, interest, dividends, profits); remittances and grants are current transfers. Flag lists that put transfers inside factor income.
Check acronyms against standard usage (screen 'NFIAD' vs usual 'NFIA').
Flag 'always' or 'never' when the same narration earlier said 'mostly'.
A sign shown in a formula must keep the algebra consistent: if NFIA is negative, write GNP = GDP + NFIA or GDP minus its size, not GDP - NFIA.
When parts of a net figure are taught, each part should get the same pattern (one inflow, one outflow, small numbers, net); flag a part that breaks the pattern (grants had no numbers).
Rows shown on screen but never spoken (NDP, NNP) should be marked 'coming next' or removed.
Live-action film clips and real company or bank logos cannot be reused; replace with generic characters and generic company/bank shapes.
Transcript gaps over 10 s during teaching must be re-transcribed before talmel scoring (152-168 s here).
No verdict mark (tick, crown, sash) may appear before the narration gives the verdict; here the tick on NNP shows at the start of a contest whose result comes 2.5 minutes later.
When a definition is spoken as a formula (NDP = GDP - depreciation), the formula must be on screen, not only a descriptive paragraph.
Key words must match between screen and voice and between cards (residents vs citizens for GNP and NNP).
When the narration announces N reasons or steps, a visible counter with N slots must be on screen and advance on each 'pehla / doosra / teesra' (worked here with the 3-step podium).

Absolute economic claims ('directly proportional', 'cannot be used') should be flagged for a fact check; e.g. GNI per capita is widely used to classify countries, and national accounts count residents, not citizens.
Definition cards over about 25 words on a character turn should be split: one picture of the rule (border, resident abroad, wear and tear) plus a 3-5 word heading.
A transcript gap over 4 s at the start of a new idea (175-180 s here) should be flagged for re-transcription before talmel is judged.

For a list of parts taught one by one, keep a side checklist that brackets the current part and ticks finished parts (worked well here); a code check can require it when a list has 3 or more items taught in sequence.
A claim that something is missing ('HDI does not capture X') must be drawn: grey out or cross the uncovered items, not just leave them unlinked.
A mapping the narrator draws between two lists (HDI dimension to component) is a claim and must be checked against a source before it is drawn.
Real photos of real people, national flags and real emblems on screen must be replaced by generic drawings; flag any photo held on screen for a long time.
A highlight that picks a subset ('only a few benefit') must land on those words, not 4.5 s before.
Do not draw an equals sign between two concepts unless the source states they are the same.
Spell-check on-screen titles ('what constitute development').
A transcript gap of more than 5 s (248-261 s) over a closing picture flags lost narration.
A worked example that sets up a formula for several inputs must compute every one of them on screen; leaving x and y (or a tick) where a number belongs fails the check.
When a formula changes for one case (log for income), the script must say why in one plain line; 'the formula will not work here' without a reason fails.
Every number on screen (band cut-offs 0.800, 0.700, 0.550) must be spoken, or the voice must point to the table and name the band in use.
A made-up example ('maan lijiye') must not carry a real country's name or flag; use a fictional country or real data, not both.
Real statistics (HDI 0.633, rank 132 of 191, 67.2 years, $6,590) must carry the report year on screen.
Term check against the source: the voice and screen say 'GNP per capita' where the UNDP method uses GNI per capita; a glossary check should flag such near-miss terms.
A spoken rule with three cases (below min, above max, in between) should be shown as three cases (a value clamped at the floor, at the ceiling, and placed between), not as one small icon.
Speech rate above about 180 words a minute with no pause over 1.2 s through formulas should flag a pacing warning for school-level learners.
A still canvas longer than about 20 s while the narration gives new causes or the key comparison must be flagged; each spoken cause (transitory factor, rain) needs its own picture.
A label must not appear long before its words: 'volatile & transitory' came 12-35 s early; keep a label within about 2 s of the term.
When the narrator asks the viewer a question, the answer text must wait for the spoken answer (here it appeared 2.7 s before).
The same item must keep one name in speech and on screen (spoken 'energy' vs on-screen 'fuel').
A comparison of two measures should carry one number example (headline x% vs core y% in the same month) so the difference is seen, not only stated.
Branded newspaper pages and real mastheads must be redrawn as generic newspapers.
Dates of policy switches written on screen (CPI-C 'since Feb 2015') must be checked against a source before reuse.
A transcript stretch of more than 5 s with no words (12.6-24.4 s, 41.3-46.6 s) flags lost or missing narration in BIE's own audio checks.
Every number written on screen must equal the spoken number (screen +289.85 vs spoken 289.95; spoken 598.95 vs screen 589.95), and every written sum must add up (-284 + 289.85 is not 5.95).
A narration stretch over 10 s with no recognised words must be flagged; if a step happens on screen inside it (futures closed at 700), its reason must be re-recorded or written into the script.

A claim like 'profit in both cases' must be checked against the mechanism: a held hedge locks the price, so any gain beyond that must come from a named choice (closing early) that carries its own risk.
A private one-to-one deal used to explain futures must be labelled a forward, with one line on what makes futures different (exchange, standard lots, daily settlement).
Titles and tree branches that promise a topic (options) must either be taught or marked 'next video' on screen.
Spell-check every on-screen title and label (DERIVATES).
No canvas may stay still for more than about 45 s while the narration introduces new ideas (215-272 s here).
A spoken what-if with its own numbers (price only 5100, buyer loses) gets its own picture, not only a sentence.
Real companies, real people, real controversies and broker app screens are replaced with generic ones before BIE uses an example.

A decorative loop (the line redrawing inside the badge) must not run under explanations: motion must mean something, e.g. the line falls when 'HPI is down' is said; a looping animation also blinds the change detector that BIE's own talmel check needs.
A spoken scenario with steps (loan, documents held, default, sale, shortfall) must be drawn step by step; adding a tick is not showing.
Real company names, real share prices and real charts may not be used as hooks; use a made-up company and avoid anything that reads as buy or sell advice.
Real people's photos must not stand in for characters (the broker), and a profession must not be drawn as a villain.
Facts about institutions' roles must be date-checked (NHB's regulatory role changed in 2019) and data-coverage claims checked against the publisher's method note.
Numbers on screen (2,544.95; chart axis and months) that are never spoken should be spoken or removed.
A video about an index must say what an index value means (base 100, a rise to 120 = prices up 20%); flag 'index' topics with no index number.
A definition given only in callout text (primary vs secondary market) needs its picture (developer -> buyer vs owner -> new buyer).

Market-wide rules must not be assigned to one institution: a claim that two depositories in one market have different settlement cycles should flag, and the settlement cycle must be checked against the current rule and dated.
Founding years and laws are checked per entity (NSDL and CDSL separately), not shared in one line.
How a financial instrument works (who issues an IDR or GDR, where the underlying shares sit, which currency) needs a source check before a scene shows money and shares moving.
A percentage split (80/20) must say 'of what' (value held or number of accounts) and give the date.
A question put to the viewer ('is money going abroad good? comment') must be answered in the video or in the notes; an open question with no answer fails.
Generic roles come first: a real brand logo must not stand for a role (depository participant); use a generic broker card.
No promotional overlay may cover teaching content while it is being recapped.
Colour identity: an object that reappears across scenes (company, its certificate, its receipt, its table row) keeps one colour; worked well here, enforce it.
When the voice describes a transfer ('our money goes ... and reaches the company'), the moving object must travel during those words and land as the destination is named (done at 283-288 s).

A ratio must be defined with its real denominator from the source (RBI's debt service ratio is over current receipts, not GDP); BIE should store each indicator's official definition and check the script against it.
When a figure is read from a chart, the spoken value must match the chart's own label (18.7% spoken vs 18.6% on the chart) or the difference must be explained (different date or source).
A chart shown with 'today's value' must reach today (a 2008-2018 chart under a 7.5% 'today' label).
Do not show a run of more than three figures before the first is explained; teach each indicator where its number first appears.
Cross-country comparisons need a like-for-like note (rich economies borrowing in their own currency) or should be left out.

Voice and screen must say the same thing (the voice says equity 'invested' by a foreign company counts as debt; the screen says 'lends'); a check should compare spoken claims with on-screen text in the same shot.
Illustrations must not put the learner's own country into a failure scene the narration says does not apply (India on the default wrecking-ball image).

A spoken 'why' with no picture (currency risk, why total debt and reserves make the two ratios close) should get a drawn cause chain; an exchange-rate change shown on the payback arrow would carry denomination risk.
Hidden gaps (one syllable stretched over 10 s or more) must be flagged in BIE's narration QA; here they hid the naming of 'fiscal deficit' and the rupee-loan case.
A worked example must reach the answer to the question it was built for: RWA 900 at 8% gives 72 of capital; stopping at 900 leaves 'how much?' unanswered.
The same quantity must not get two values in one script (tier 1 minimum '4%' under Basel II, then 'previously 4.5%' under Basel III).
Every number on screen must be spoken (CRAR 9%) and every number spoken that matters must be shown (tier 1 4.5% to 6%, LCR 100%).

The label read out for a data chart must match the chart's own title (a 'Tier I leverage ratio' chart read as tier 1 capital); an achieved ratio from a report must not be called a requirement set by RBI.

Regulatory facts must be checked against the regulator's source before narration: Basel III tier 3, the 9.5% total, India's adoption year, what counts as disclosed reserves, where retained earnings and fixed assets belong, and the example's risk weights.
When the voice describes an action on a metaphor object (break the piggy bank, tow the car, close the jar's lid), the object must do it on screen on that word.
A metaphor set works when all objects appear together first, each is then lifted into a focus panel and returned, and they all come back together at the end (keep this pattern).
BIE's narration QA should flag a single word stretched over more than 3 s as a hidden gap (here 77-89 s) as well as normal silences.
Every number drawn on screen (10 Cr loan, 24.8%, 2.5%, 2.78% March 2023) must be spoken, or labelled with its source and date; a current-value figure must be checked against the source for that date.
A spoken story longer than about 15 s must get its own picture (here the promoter misuse story ran 27 s over a still list).
With a process map that returns between steps, the marker must land on the step's naming word (within about 0.8 s); here it led by up to 5 s.
Legal process facts (appeal forums, withdrawal rule, vote threshold for approving a plan) must be checked against the law's text and flagged for review before narration.
Acronyms recalled from earlier lessons must each get a one-line meaning, or be dropped from the recall.
No overlay (promotion, banner) may cover the teaching diagram while a fact on it is being spoken.
When a rule exists to stop a misuse, the narration must say who loses from the misuse, not only that it was misuse.
A transcript gap of more than 4 s right after a picture change flags a line to re-check in the narration audio.

games.player_does: Is the entrepreneur of a one-laptop country: rents land, hires workers, borrows capital and pays each factor by dragging coins, then sets the laptop's price and sells it to a buyer.
games.process_happens: Each payment fills a factor reward (rent, wages, interest, profit) and builds the laptop's cost; when the buyer pays, three meters fill: total income, total product value, total spending.
games.win: All three meters show the same number.
games.lose: Setting a price above what was paid out leaves a gap between meters that is labelled 'this extra is also someone's income: profit'; once profit is counted the meters match again.
games.concept: income = products = expenditure

games.player_does: Matches each factor of production to its reward: land, labour, capital, entrepreneur with rent, wages, interest, profit.
games.process_happens: A correct match draws a blue arrow from the factor into the laptop and puts the reward on the income band.
games.win: All four matched and the laptop is built.
games.lose: A wrong pair (land with interest) makes that worker or owner walk off, and the laptop stays half built, with the right pair shown.
games.concept: factors of production and their rewards

games.player_does: Taps people to add their incomes: first oneself, then family members, then rows of people across the map, keeping a running sum.
games.process_happens: Each tapped person's income flies into the sum; at country scale the sum becomes the NATIONAL INCOME chip and the equation appears beside it.
games.win: Reach the country total and predict that the product and spending totals will be the same.
games.lose: Counting someone outside the border shows the person standing outside the map with a 'not inside the territory' note.
games.concept: national income as the sum of everyone's income

games.player_does: Is the central bank and turns an inflation dial each year to cut unemployment.
games.process_happens: In the short run the dot climbs the curve and the unemployment bar shrinks; after a few years wage-demand cards play (prices up, workers ask for raises, firms cannot pay all, firing) and the dot slides back to the natural rate while inflation stays high; pushing harder piles up hatch lines without moving the dot.
games.win: Keep unemployment at the natural rate with steady inflation for ten years (find NAIRU).
games.lose: Pushing unemployment below the natural rate makes the inflation meter run away while unemployment returns, which teaches the long-run critique.
games.concept: short-run trade-off vs long-run natural rate (NAIRU)

games.player_does: Orders cards to explain why the trade-off breaks: high inflation, higher living costs, demand for higher wages, firms cannot pay everyone, firing, unemployment back to the natural rate.
games.process_happens: Each correct card moves the dot one step back along the curve and writes the step in the chain box.
games.win: Dot back at the natural rate with the chain complete.
games.lose: A card out of order freezes the dot and shows which earlier step is missing.
games.concept: why the trade-off fails in the long run

games.player_does: Places idea cards on a timeline: 1950s thesis on UK data, 1958 publication, 1960s fame, early 1970s challenge, natural rate and NAIRU.
games.process_happens: Each placed card changes the curve on screen: it appears, grows famous (gets a crown), gets a 'short term' label, then the label is struck and 'long term' and NAIRU appear.
games.win: Timeline complete and the final curve matches the video's last picture.
games.lose: Putting the challenge before the publication shows a crossed-out curve with nothing to challenge yet.
games.concept: the life of the Phillips curve idea

games.player_does: Plays RBI at the list desk: bank cards show paid-up capital, reserves, liquidity and solvency; the player decides which banks go into Schedule II under the current criteria. An 'economy event' card then changes the criteria.
games.process_happens: A cash crunch follows: listed banks draw cheap repo loans (green note riding the RBI arrow), unlisted ones must borrow from the market or pay a red higher emergency rate; customer stars drift toward listed banks.
games.win: The list matches the criteria after every change and no weak bank fails in the crunch.
games.lose: Listing a weak bank makes it fail in the crunch (why the criteria exist); leaving a strong bank off makes it pay a high rate and lose customers (why the status matters).
games.concept: Schedule II criteria and the benefits of scheduled status

games.player_does: Drags bank cards (a public sector bank, an RRB, a small finance bank, a payments bank, a local area bank, a foreign bank) into a tree: scheduled or unscheduled, then commercial or co-operative.
games.process_happens: Each correct drop grows a leaf on the tree the way the video does.
games.win: Every card placed in a branch where it is allowed.
games.lose: Dropping a public sector bank or RRB on the unscheduled side bounces it back with the rule; a payments bank on the unscheduled side is accepted but tagged 'none today'.
games.concept: types of banks

games.player_does: Starts at Economic Growth and drags 'depends on' cards to the left one by one: price stability, inflation, demand, purchasing power, money, liquid money.
games.process_happens: Each correct card snaps in with its arrow pointing toward the effect; when liquid money is placed, the RBI CONTROL arms slide under it and the chain folds into the MONETARY POLICY badge.
games.win: Chain complete and the badge formed.
games.lose: A card placed with the arrow the wrong way plays the wrong claim aloud (for example 'inflation creates money') and shows the contradiction on the chain.
games.concept: root cause of inflation and what monetary policy controls

games.player_does: Holds a wallet of assets (5 crore house, FD, PF, PPF, cash, savings account) and must buy a 25 lakh plane offered for one day only; chooses which assets to use.
games.process_happens: Blocked assets show 'months' timers and a rival with cash takes the plane; liquid assets complete the purchase, the demand meter rises and the price meter ticks up.
games.win: Buy in time using only liquid money and sort every asset into blocked or liquid.
games.lose: Choosing the house or FD shows the rival flying off with the plane, with the note 'rich on paper, no purchasing power today'.
games.concept: blocked vs liquid money and why only liquid money makes demand

games.player_does: Seats six people at the MPC table: the RBI Governor in the chair, a Deputy Governor, a nominated RBI official, and three members from the government side.
games.process_happens: Each correct seat lights a member; when all six are seated, the committee gets a liquid-money tap with a dotted (indirect) and a solid (direct) handle.
games.win: Correct committee, then bring inflation into a target band by turning the right handle.
games.lose: Putting a government member in the chair shows the [Chairman] tag jumping back to the Governor.
games.concept: MPC composition and direct vs indirect tools

games.player_does: Fills the basket: sets each partner's weight from a trade-share bar (they must add to 100%) and drags in each partner's per-rupee rate.
games.process_happens: Each row computes weight x rate in the answer column; the column sums into the NEER number, which hangs from the basket tied to the rupee note.
games.win: Reach the target NEER for the given year with weights that match the trade shares.
games.lose: Weights that do not add to 100% leave the basket lopsided and the NEER cell blank; a wrong product lights that row red.
games.concept: how NEER is calculated

games.player_does: Moves a NEER slider up or down and predicts what happens to the rupee and to the trade deficit before the system plays it.
games.process_happens: NEER up: the rupee note rises against the basket, exports shrink, the deficit bar grows; NEER down: the reverse.
games.win: Predict all four links correctly for both directions.
games.lose: A wrong prediction replays the chain with the mismatched link highlighted.
games.concept: NEER, appreciation/depreciation and the trade deficit

games.player_does: Runs India's exports to the US while the rupee stays pegged to the partner basket; rival exporters (China, Indonesia) can depreciate against the dollar.
games.process_happens: When a rival depreciates, its goods get cheaper on the US shelf, India's orders fall, the reserve meter drains toward a BoP crisis; the learner can hold the peg or devalue in steps.
games.win: Keep exports and reserves alive, which needs a timely two-step devaluation.
games.lose: Holding the peg too long shows India's shelf emptying and a BoP crisis banner, as in 1991.
games.concept: why the basket peg failed and led to the 1991 devaluation

games.player_does: Places regimes on a 1944-today strip: Bretton Woods (to 1971), peg to pound (1971-75), basket/NEER peg (1975-92), LERMS (1992-93), floating (1993-).
games.process_happens: The strip colours green for fixed and blue for floating as cards land, with the 1991 devaluation marker.
games.win: Strip complete and two-coloured correctly.
games.lose: Placing floating before LERMS shows the next-lesson note: LERMS needs floating explained first, but came first in time.
games.concept: India's exchange-rate regimes over time

games.player_does: For each scenario card (boom, slump, oil shock), sets an up or down arrow under GDP, inflation and unemployment before the system plays it.
games.process_happens: The economy flow runs the scenario: factories hire or fire, wages and prices move, and the table row fills with the real directions.
games.win: All three arrows right for every scenario.
games.lose: Using the normal rule on the oil shock (inflation down because GDP is down) turns the row red with a big '?', and the oil barrel's cost band on raw material shows why prices rose anyway.
games.concept: normal pattern vs stagflation

games.player_does: Builds the oil-shock chain by dragging cards onto the economy flow: oil price up, raw-material cost up, production cost up, prices up, demand down, growth slows, GDP down, unemployment up.
games.process_happens: Each placed card lights its node on the flow and the meter it touches moves (price meter up, GDP meter down).
games.win: The finished chain ends with both the price meter up and the GDP meter down: the STAGFLATION tag lights.
games.lose: A card in the wrong place makes a meter move the wrong way, and the narrator line explains which link was skipped.
games.concept: cost-push cause of stagflation

games.player_does: Runs a factory in a growing economy and decides wages each quarter to keep and attract workers while rivals bid for the same staff.
games.process_happens: Higher wages raise unit cost; the player chooses whether to raise shelf prices; the town's price level and unemployment meters update.
games.win: Stay staffed and profitable through the boom.
games.lose: Keeping wages low loses workers to rivals; raising them without raising prices wipes out profit, showing why boom wages end up as inflation.
games.concept: GDP growth -> low unemployment -> wage-cost inflation

games.player_does: Sets trade weights for six partner currencies (must total 100%), then sees one month's exchange-rate moves and calls whether the rupee appreciated or depreciated; in level two, switches on each country's inflation.
games.process_happens: The table multiplies and adds live and shows NEER and its change; in level two the REAL column fills, REER appears beside NEER, and the rupee coin grows or shrinks against the basket.
games.win: Correct appreciation / depreciation calls for five months, and a correct prediction of whether REER ends above or below NEER.
games.lose: Weights not adding to 100% lock the sum; calling 'appreciated' when NEER fell shows the rupee coin shrinking against the basket; ignoring inflation shows REER drifting away from NEER.
games.concept: NEER calculation, its reading, and REER

games.player_does: Matches parts of the inflation toolkit to their currency twins: basket of goods to basket of currencies, price change to exchange-rate change, consumption weight to trade weight, CPI/WPI question to NEER/REER question.
games.process_happens: Each correct pair lights up both panels side by side, as in the video's mirrored layout.
games.win: All pairs matched.
games.lose: Pairing 'basket of goods' with 'inflation adjustment' shows the mismatch: the currency basket holds currencies weighted by trade.
games.concept: need for a currency index (analogy with CPI/WPI)

games.player_does: Plays a small investor over many quarters: the economy line moves (mostly up) while event cards arrive (bad news about a company, a war abroad, an RBI rate change, neighbours boasting about gains); each turn chooses buy, hold or sell.
games.process_happens: Crowd moods (panic, fear of missing out) push the stock-market line away from the economy line for a few turns, then it drifts back to follow the economy.
games.win: End with more wealth than a 'panic seller' bot by holding through short dips that the economy line does not share.
games.lose: Selling on a one-off news dip locks in the loss, and the replay shows the market rejoining the economy line soon after.
games.concept: long-run link vs short-term disconnect; market sentiment

games.player_does: Drags cards into order between Economy and Stock Market: people earn more, spending up, demand up, prices up, sales and profits up, profits reinvested, market up.
games.process_happens: Each correct link sends a chevron along the band and lifts the market lens chart a little.
games.win: A complete chain lifts the market chart to the top.
games.lose: Placing a wrong card (for example 'demand down') breaks the flow and the lens chart dips, showing prices falling instead.
games.concept: reason 1: customer spending chain

games.player_does: Holds a bond with face value 1000 and coupon 100 a year; each round the market price moves with demand and supply, and the player decides to keep, sell or buy another.
games.process_happens: The bond moves along the chain of holders and the coupon arrow follows whoever holds it; under each holder a yield column shows 100 / price paid as a percent.
games.win: End with a yield above the coupon rate by buying below face value.
games.lose: Buying above face value shows the yield column below the coupon rate, with 'price up, yield down' lit.
games.concept: bond yield vs coupon rate (inverse to price)

games.player_does: Splits savings across bonds of several companies, each shown with a rating on the green-to-red ladder and a coupon rate (lower-rated pay more).
games.process_happens: Years pass; coupons arrive by dotted arrows; some low-rated companies 'run away' or go bankrupt and their arrows stop and the principal vanishes.
games.win: Get back all principal with steady coupons.
games.lose: Chasing the highest coupon on red-rated bonds loses principal, showing why the rating matters.
games.concept: default risk and credit rating agencies

games.player_does: Sorts deals into primary or secondary market: company sells new bonds to you, you sell to a friend on the stock exchange, a fund buys from another investor, the company issues a second batch.
games.process_happens: Each card lights the matching part of the chain (cream panel for company-to-first-investor, blue panel for investor-to-investor) and moves the sidebar box.
games.win: All deals placed correctly.
games.lose: A wrong card lights the panel on the wrong link and shows who the seller is in that deal.
games.concept: primary vs secondary market, selling on the stock exchange

games.player_does: Runs the only ketchup factory in the country for a year: sets how many bottles to make and their price, and watches the machine work.
games.process_happens: The machine's value bar drops by its depreciation as it runs; at year end the player fills the Gross Produce and Net Produce chips and the system checks them (gross = bottles x price, net = gross - depreciation).
games.win: Both chips right, and the NDP equation lights with the player's own numbers.
games.lose: Leaving depreciation out makes net equal gross; the machine's lost value flashes in red beside the chip as the missing deduction.
games.concept: net = gross - depreciation (NDP)

games.player_does: Drags items into 'counts for NDP' or 'does not count': factory machine, delivery van, phone used for business, phone used personally, family car, office laptop.
games.process_happens: Each item travels the YES path into the depreciation column or stops at a crossed NO, as in the video.
games.win: All items sorted.
games.lose: Putting the family car in 'counts' shows its NO path, with the note that only assets used to produce goods and services count.
games.concept: which depreciation counts in NDP and NNP

games.player_does: As the farmer, decides how much of the harvest to keep back as seed for next season before selling the rest.
games.process_happens: The sack splits into 'seed kept' and 'available'; the Gross Produce and Net Produce chips fill with the harvest and harvest minus seed.
games.win: Keep enough seed to repeat the harvest and read off the net produce correctly.
games.lose: Keeping no seed shows next season's empty field, which teaches why the input must be deducted to see what was truly produced.
games.concept: gross vs net produce

games.player_does: Plays RBI with two dials, repo rate and reverse repo rate, and a target (inflation high: cool lending; slowdown: boost lending). Banks decide each round whether to borrow from RBI or park surplus with it.
games.process_happens: Arrows animate: solid loans flow down at the repo %, dotted parked money flows up at the reverse repo %; each bank's liquidity bar fills or drains and its loans to people grow or shrink.
games.win: Bring lending to the target zone by moving both rates the right way.
games.lose: Cutting rates during high inflation floods banks with liquidity and the loan arrows to people multiply; the panel shows 'rates down, liquidity up'.
games.concept: cutting or raising both rates raises or lowers liquidity

games.player_does: Plays a bank short of cash for one night: drags 100 rupees of government securities to RBI and signs the agreement, then next day buys them back.
games.process_happens: RBI pays 100 minus one day's interest at the chosen repo rate; the next day the bank pays 100 and gets its securities back; the gap is shown as RBI's earning; the word 'repurchase' lights up on the agreement.
games.win: Meet the night's shortfall and correctly state who buys back what.
games.lose: Trying to keep the securities after the date shows the agreement clause and a penalty; mixing up who repurchases flips the arrows and shows the reverse repo instead.
games.concept: repurchase agreement: securities as collateral, sale and buy-back, name unpacked

games.player_does: Given a bank's NDTL (for example 2000 crore) and a cash need, chooses how much to take by repo, term repo and LTRO.
games.process_happens: Limit bars fill: 0.25% of NDTL for repo (5 crore), 0.75% for term repo (15 crore), with durations shown (overnight, 7-28 days, 1-3 years).
games.win: Cover the need within all limits with durations that match it.
games.lose: Asking past a limit is refused with the % rule shown; using overnight repo for a 2-year need shows the bank having to roll over every night.
games.concept: borrowing limits as % of NDTL with worked numbers (2000 crore)

games.player_does: Sets each year's inflation rate with a slider, year after year.
games.process_happens: The price-index curve grows; each new stretch is coloured by itself: yellow INFLATION when the rate is positive, green DISINFLATION when it is positive but lower than last year, pink DEFLATION when it goes below zero.
games.win: Draw what a mission asks, for example 'bring inflation down from 7% to 3% without deflation'.
games.lose: Pushing the rate below zero turns the stretch pink and opens the deflation chain (buyers wait, demand falls), so the learner sees that slowing inflation is not the same as falling prices.
games.concept: inflation vs disinflation vs deflation

games.player_does: Plays the government in a town where prices keep falling and shoppers say 'next month it will be cheaper'; picks policy cards: raise public spending, cut taxes, cut interest rates, or wrong cards such as raise taxes.
games.process_happens: Right cards push the price level up, shoppers start buying, profits recover, layoffs stop and the NPA meter falls; the word REFLATION lands when the curve turns up.
games.win: Stop the slide and get the price-index curve rising gently again.
games.lose: A wrong card deepens the chain one step (demand down, then profits, then jobs and loans), showing each link of why deflation hurts.
games.concept: why deflation hurts and how reflation works

games.player_does: Colours stretches of a real price-index chart with three markers.
games.process_happens: Each marked stretch gets its label and tick sticker as in the video; the slope of the stretch is shown beside the choice.
games.win: Every stretch marked correctly.
games.lose: Marking a rising-but-slower stretch as deflation shows the line still going up, with the note that prices fall only when the line goes down.
games.concept: spotting the phases on real data

games.player_does: Runs a one-product economy for five years, setting how many laptops are made and the inflation rate each year.
games.process_happens: The table fills (quantity, price, GDP); the GDP block grows with a yellow inflation stripe; a second block shows real GDP at base-year prices.
games.win: Make real GDP grow three years in a row (more laptops), not just nominal GDP.
games.lose: Raising only inflation makes nominal GDP climb while real GDP stays flat; the 'inflated GDP' tag appears and the stripe fills the block.
games.concept: nominal GDP vs real GDP

games.player_does: Reads news-style claims ('GDP up 12%, so we made 12% more goods') with the year's inflation given, and taps the error.
games.process_happens: The stripe slides out of the GDP block, showing how much of the rise was inflation and how much was real; arcs hop back to the base year.
games.win: Correctly split each rise into inflation and real growth.
games.lose: Accepting the claim shows the stripe still inside the block and the real growth much smaller than claimed.
games.concept: removing inflation back to a base year

games.player_does: Places cards (real/nominal, factor cost/market price, constant/current prices, includes taxes/excludes) onto the four-leaf GDP tree.
games.process_happens: Each leaf fills; when all four are right, India's leaf (nominal at market price) lights with the 'kyun?' tag.
games.win: All four leaves correctly built and India's choice found.
games.lose: Putting 'constant prices' under nominal flashes the inflation stripe back into the block.
games.concept: four ways of calculating GDP; India's choice

games.player_does: Drags each next quarter's GDP point up or down on the chart, quarter by quarter.
games.process_happens: The step frame lands on the new piece and labels it (growing faster, growing slower, contraction); two falling quarters in a row shade a red RECESSION band by themselves; a long red run turns into DEPRESSION.
games.win: Draw the pattern a mission asks for, for example 'slow the economy down without a contraction' or 'a recession that recovers before it becomes a depression'.
games.lose: Pulling a point below the last one when slower growth was asked shows a CONTRACTION label, so the learner feels the line between slower growth and an actual fall.
games.concept: growth vs slower growth vs contraction vs recession vs depression

games.player_does: Gets short runs of quarterly GDP numbers and sorts each run into growth, slower growth, contraction, recession or depression.
games.process_happens: Each sorted run is drawn as a curve with the frame or band the video uses.
games.win: All runs sorted correctly.
games.lose: A single falling quarter put under recession shows only one red piece, with the note that recession needs two in a row.
games.concept: recession as two contractions in a row

games.player_does: Runs the one bread shop: each day an event card hits (more buyers arrive, a packet is lost, the factory raises its price), the learner sets the day's price and then tags the cause as demand-pull, bottleneck or cost-push.
games.process_happens: Buyers with 'ready to pay' tags line up; at the learner's price the packets move to the buyers who can pay and crosses fall under the rest; the node that changed (demand, supply, cost) lights up on the supply - price - demand line.
games.win: Sell out every day without losing money and tag every cause correctly.
games.lose: Too low a price leaves a long queue and an empty shelf; too high leaves bread unsold; a wrong tag replays the day highlighting the node that really changed.
games.concept: demand-pull vs bottleneck vs cost-push

games.player_does: Sorts news cards (festival crowds rush the market, a flood ruins the wheat crop, bakery wages rise, a sudden ban on a raw material, a cash bonus for every family) into demand-pull, bottleneck (structural) and cost-push.
games.process_happens: Each card, when dropped, plays on the bread-shop scene: buyers multiply, packets vanish, or the factory's cost chip rises, and the price tag moves.
games.win: All cards placed with the matching scene change.
games.lose: Putting the flood under cost-push shows that only the shelf emptied while the factory cost stayed the same, with a nudge to look at the supply node.
games.concept: classifying causes of inflation

games.player_does: Controls how much money is in the two buyers' wallets while the factory raises its cost and the shopkeeper tries 55.
games.process_happens: With no extra money the buyers refuse 55 and bread sits unsold until the price falls back; with fuller wallets 55 sticks; adding money with no cost change also pulls the price up.
games.win: Show a price rise that lasts, and notice it lasts only when wallets grow.
games.lose: Raising cost alone shows the price spike and fall back, with the Monetarist note 'cost-push is not independent'.
games.concept: Monetarist view: inflation needs more money in people's hands

games.player_does: Watches a basket of eight goods month by month with only the overall price gauge visible; can 'open the basket' (costs a turn) to see each item's arrow; each month calls it: normal, inflation, deflation or skewflation.
games.process_happens: Item arrows grow by different amounts and the overall chip shows their weighted average; in some months two items (food) race ahead while the average stays normal.
games.win: Call skewflation in the right months and name the racing items.
games.lose: Calling skewflation when every item rises together shows that this is plain inflation; watching only the gauge and missing the racing items replays the 2009-10 case (WPI calm, food above 20%).
games.concept: skewflation vs inflation

games.player_does: Sets how much each of eight goods' price rises this year.
games.process_happens: The arrows grow to match and the overall price chip moves to their average; the tree under the basket lights inflation, deflation or neither.
games.win: Hit a target overall inflation with at least one item falling, showing items can disagree with the total.
games.lose: If two items are pushed far above the rest while the total stays on target, the screen flags skewflation instead of a pass.
games.concept: overall vs individual prices

games.player_does: Runs a bank with NDTL 2000 crore for one day. Customers arrive with loan requests (5, 10, 20, 40 crore); when spare cash runs out, the player chooses a source: repo, term repo or MSF, and drags G-secs to RBI as collateral.
games.process_happens: The G-sec moves up to RBI, a loan comes down the matching channel with its rate, and the loan goes out to the customer; limit bars fill (5 crore repo, 15 crore term repo, 20 crore MSF from the SLR safe).
games.win: Serve all customers at the lowest interest cost: repo first, then term repo, MSF only for the last 20 crore.
games.lose: Going to MSF while repo room is left charges the penalty and shows RBI's 'careless bank' stamp; asking past 1% of NDTL under MSF is refused with the limit shown on the magnifier.
games.concept: MSF: overnight loan against SLR securities, up to 1% of NDTL

games.player_does: Splits a bank's NDTL into CRR (RBI vault), SLR (cash, gold or securities), loans and idle money, with customers arriving at random.
