games.player_does: Acts as a newspaper editor: given a month's headline and core figures and a news ticker (vegetable prices up 30%), chooses which number goes on the front page and writes the cause under it.
games.process_happens: The front page prints the chosen figure; a reader asks 'is inflation really rising long-term?' and the core line answers.
games.win: Headline figure on the front page, food spike named as the cause, core named as the long-run trend.
games.lose: Printing core as 'headline' or calling a one-month food spike a long-run trend shows the trend line flat and the reader misled.
games.concept: headline vs core: total inflation vs long-run trend

games.player_does: Places index chips (WPI, CPI-Combined) on India's timeline as the headline measure.
games.process_happens: The newspaper icon above the timeline changes which index it quotes as the chip is placed.
games.win: WPI before the switch, CPI-C after it, with the switch dated (date to be checked: April 2014 adoption, February 2015 agreement).
games.lose: A wrong order makes the newspaper quote a wholesale index for a consumer price story, and the mismatch is pointed out.
games.concept: India's headline index: WPI till 2014, CPI-C from Feb 2015

games.player_does: Plays the buyer whose salary comes in 30 days. A banner warns prices may rise. The player either waits or signs a contract with the shoe owner at a chosen price (5200, 5500, 6000), then the 30-day price is drawn (5100, 6000, 8000 or 10000).
games.process_happens: The contract document drops between the two, cash and token cross the band on day 30, and a meter shows what the player paid against the market price; a 'peace' meter stays full for the contract holder while it swings for the waiter.
games.win: Can always buy the shoes on day 30 and the price paid never exceeds the budget.
games.lose: Waiting and drawing 8000 or 10000 leaves the player unable to buy (the crying scene returns); signing and drawing 5100 shows the 400 paid for certainty, so the learner sees a hedge has a cost.
games.concept: futures agreement: price and date fixed today, both sides bound

games.player_does: Holds 100 shares bought at 584 of a generic company with bad news on the ticker; decides whether to sell month-end futures at 590, then watches the price path play to the expiry date; may also choose to close the futures early.
games.process_happens: Two bars move together: share profit/loss and futures profit/loss, with a net bar between them; on the expiry date the futures price meets the share price and the position is squared off.
games.win: Hedged to expiry, the net bar stays near the locked value whether the path ends at 300 or 984.
games.lose: Unhedged, the falling path shows a 284-per-share loss; closing the futures early and then seeing the price fall back shows that lifting a hedge is a bet, not hedging.
games.concept: hedging a share with a futures sell: rising case and closing the futures early

games.player_does: Matches each derivative card (temple token, gold futures, a currency contract, a share futures) to its underlying asset (shoes, gold, dollars, shares) and then changes the asset's price with a slider.
games.process_happens: The matched card's value moves with the asset's price, struck and rewritten like the token.
games.win: All pairs matched so every derivative's value follows its slider.
games.lose: A wrong pair shows a derivative whose value does not move when 'its' asset moves, which breaks the definition.
games.concept: underlying assets and derivatives as financial instruments

games.player_does: Works as a bank's home-loan officer: each applicant brings a house, its asking price and the area's HPI line; the player approves or rejects the loan amount.
games.process_happens: Approved loans run forward a few years; some buyers default, the bank takes the documents, sells the house at the area's HPI price and the shortfall or surplus shows in the bank's vault.
games.win: Lend only up to the HPI-backed value, so every forced sale covers the loan.
games.lose: Approving an overpriced house shows the forced sale falling short and the vault losing money: the reason lenders check HPI.
games.concept: why lenders check HPI: the house as loan security

games.player_does: Owns a house and must sell within two years; each month sees the city's HPI line and a broker's offer, and decides to sell now or wait.
games.process_happens: The HPI line moves month by month; offers above the trend come from a pushy broker on the buying side, offers below it when the market is down.
games.win: Sell when the line is up and the offer matches the area value; spot a broker's inflated quote when buying the next house.
games.lose: Selling in a dip shows the loss against the trend; accepting the broker's inflated price on the next purchase shows how much was overpaid.
games.concept: HPI for buyers and sellers: informed decisions

games.player_does: Sorts house-sale cards (builder sells a new flat; family resells its flat; builder sells in a small town; owner resells in a metro) into primary and secondary market, then into the index that counts them as the video describes.
games.process_happens: Each card drops into its market bin; the two index badges light up for the sales they include.
games.win: All cards in the right market bin (developer to buyer = primary, owner to new buyer = secondary).
games.lose: A resale placed in 'primary' shows the developer missing from the deal; keep the index-coverage step marked 'check source' until verified.
games.concept: NHB vs RBI coverage; primary vs secondary market

games.player_does: Sells 100 shares twice: first in the paper era (carry the certificate to the exchange, wait for the buyer's payment and the transfer), then in demat mode (place a sell order from a demat account).
games.process_happens: Paper mode: the certificate travels slowly, random events strike (certificate lost, forged signature, a fee for courier and stamping); demat mode: the depository moves 100 shares from the seller's account to the buyer's on a T+1 calendar.
games.win: Complete both sales and compare: time, cost and risk meters show why demat replaced paper.
games.lose: In paper mode, losing the certificate freezes the sale until a duplicate is issued; the game then shows the same sale finishing in demat in one day.
games.concept: depository and dematerialisation

games.player_does: Builds the path from a new investor to owning a share by placing the pieces in order: person, depository participant (generic broker or bank), demat account, exchange, clearing and settlement, depository record.
games.process_happens: Once the path is complete, an order runs along it: money goes up to the exchange, and the share appears as an entry in the investor's demat account at the depository.
games.win: The order completes and the share appears in the demat account.
games.lose: Skipping the DP or the demat account blocks the order at the exchange gate with 'no account'; putting the depository before the exchange shows a record with no trade behind it.
games.concept: depository participants and the demat account

games.player_does: Gets investor cards (a buyer in Mumbai paying rupees, a buyer in New York paying dollars, a fund in London paying euros or dollars) and drops each on the receipt it would use: IDR, ADR or GDR.
games.process_happens: The receipt slip forms in the right colour, with the currency coin and the market where it trades.
games.win: Every investor gets the right receipt and currency.
games.lose: A wrong drop shows the mismatch (an ADR asked for in rupees bounces off the dollar coin). The game must be built on a checked description of each receipt, not on this video's GDR and IDR wording.
games.concept: types of depository receipt: IDR, ADR, GDR

games.player_does: Runs India's foreign-borrowing desk for ten years: picks loans from lender cards (long-term World Bank loan, short-term commercial credit, concessional aid, tied loan, dollar or rupee denominated) to fund a budget gap each year.
games.process_happens: Meters move live: debt to GDP, debt service ratio, short-term debt to forex reserves; a shock card (oil price jump, rupee fall, capital outflow) arrives at random and the repayment bill for dollar and short-term loans rises.
games.win: Finish ten years with all ratios in the safe zone and no missed payment.
games.lose: Too much short-term or dollar debt: a shock makes payments exceed reserves, the payback arrow gets a red cross, the credit rating drops, the spread on new loans jumps, and the country must restructure.
games.concept: loan types and short-term debt ratios

games.player_does: Is a country deciding whether to repay or skip a foreign loan instalment, then tries to borrow again.
games.process_happens: Skipping lowers the credit rating badge; the next loan's interest is built live as benchmark (same for all) + spread (grows as the rating falls); the currency meter wobbles.
games.win: Keep the rating and borrow at benchmark plus a small spread.
games.lose: Two skips push the spread so high no lender offers a loan; only the 'restructure' door stays open, and some foreign assets have to be handed to creditors.
games.concept: interest = benchmark + spread

games.player_does: Drags borrowing events into 'counts as India's external debt' or 'does not': government loan from World Bank, RBI borrowing abroad, an Indian bank's dollar bond, an Indian company's foreign loan, a foreign parent lending to its Indian subsidiary, a foreign company buying shares in its Indian unit, a loan from an Indian bank.
games.process_happens: Correct items add their amount to the external-debt total and to the right slice of a borrower pie (government, RBI, banks, companies, inter-company lending).
games.win: The pie matches the official make-up: companies the largest slice, government about a fifth.
games.lose: Counting equity investment or domestic loans inflates the total and the check shows why only debt owed abroad counts.
games.concept: who in India borrows abroad

games.player_does: Chooses the currency for a 100-unit loan (dollars or rupees) and then watches the exchange rate move.
games.process_happens: If the rupee weakens, the rupee cost of the dollar repayment grows on the payback arrow; the rupee loan's repayment stays the same.
games.win: Keeps enough loans in rupees, or enough dollar reserves, that a rupee fall does not swamp repayments.
games.lose: All-dollar borrowing plus a sharp rupee fall makes the repayment balloon past the budget.
games.concept: denomination of debt

games.player_does: Runs a bank's loan book: drags each new loan card (government bond, home loan, secured business loan, unsecured personal loan) into its risk category, then sets how much capital to put in the jar as a percentage of RWA.
games.process_happens: The RWA meter adds each loan times its weight (1000 at 50% shows 500); the jar shows the capital needed at 8% (or India's 9%); random default shocks hit, and the jar absorbs them or runs dry.
games.win: Survive a run of default shocks with the jar never empty while keeping as much money lent out as possible.
games.lose: Putting a risky loan in a low-risk row understates RWA, the jar is too small, and the first big default empties it: the bank fails and depositors queue outside.
games.concept: worked RWA example (1000 and 4000 Rs to 900 Rs)

games.player_does: Faces losses of different sizes and chooses which capital layer absorbs each: the front guard (tier 1) or the airbags (tier 2).
games.process_happens: Small losses absorbed by tier 1 leave the bank open and the guard is rebuilt; using tier 2 saves the depositors, but the bank's doors close and it is towed away.
games.win: Keep the bank open through a year of shocks by holding enough tier 1.
games.lose: Relying on tier 2 for a small loss shuts the bank needlessly; too little tier 1 forces tier 2 and closure.
games.concept: tier 1 vs tier 2 capital

games.player_does: Plays RBI across an economic cycle (boom, slowdown, crisis) and decides when banks must fill the piggy bank (CCCB) and when to let them break it.
games.process_happens: Filling in the boom slows runaway lending a little; breaking it in the crisis releases capital so banks keep lending; credit and failure meters move.
games.win: The piggy bank is full when the crisis arrives and released at once, so lending does not collapse.
games.lose: Filling it during the crisis squeezes credit when it is most needed; never filling it leaves nothing to release and banks fail.
games.concept: CCCB: fill in good times, release in bad

games.player_does: Builds the bank's support: places pillars (minimum capital, supervisory review, market discipline) and drops the five containers (CAR, LCR, NSFR, CCCB, CCB) under the right accord and time horizon.
games.process_happens: Each correct placement lights the risk it covers in the sidebar; LCR survives a 30-day storm, NSFR a 1-year one.
games.win: All three risks lit and every container on its accord and horizon.
games.lose: A bank on one pillar wobbles when a market shock arrives; LCR alone cannot get it through a year-long storm.
games.concept: Basel III: iron pillar and five containers

games.player_does: Plays the lender bank whose 10 crore loan to a factory has turned NPA and pushes the case file along the six-dot CIRP board against a 330-day clock: files at an NCLT bench, appoints an insolvency professional into the factory, gathers the creditor banks into a committee, opens bidding, holds the vote, and asks NCLT to approve and monitor.
games.process_happens: At each dot the right body lights up (NCLT tags on admission, approval and monitoring); the professional's arrival stops the factory's value meter from falling; bidders' plans fly to the committee; the vote bar fills; the calendar counts down (14 days for admission, 330 in all).
games.win: A plan approved by the committee's vote and by NCLT before day 330, with the recovered amount shown back at the bank.
games.lose: Taking a step out of order (voting before the committee exists, going to NCLAT before NCLT decides) is refused; running past 330 days pushes the company towards liquidation and the bank recovers far less.
games.concept: IBC 2016 and CIRP as a step-by-step process

games.player_does: Screens bidder cards at the committee's door (a clean investor, a wilful defaulter, a person jailed three years, an investor with his own NPA account, the company's own promoter, an undischarged insolvent) and lets each in or keeps it out.
games.process_happens: Admitted bidders' plans go to the vote; a wrongly admitted one is caught at NCLT approval and the plan is struck out, losing days on the clock.
games.win: Only eligible bidders reach the vote and the plan passes NCLT first time.
games.lose: Letting the defaulting promoter in replays the misuse story: he buys back his own company cheaply, the bank's recovery meter drops, and the 2017 amendment stamp appears to explain why it is barred.
games.concept: ineligible resolution applicants

games.player_does: Drags six step chips onto the dots of an empty timeline and pins 'NCLT', 'IP' and 'CoC' tags onto the steps where each acts.
games.process_happens: Correctly placed chips lock and the ring runs along the line once all are in; each tag pinned on the right dot shows that body's action as a short animation.
games.win: All six steps in order and every tag on its step.
games.lose: A tag on the wrong step (for example the committee approving the plan instead of NCLT) shows the case bouncing back with the correct body named.

best.why: Turns the word 'Product' in GDP's name into a puzzle, so the rest of the video answers a question the learner now holds.
My income, then my family's, then the country's: a sum the learner already knows how to do grows into national income.
A one-laptop economy makes the three-way equality checkable with four small numbers.
The same 10,000 lands on spending, products and income one after another, which proves the claim on the picture itself.
A dot climbing the curve while both axis bars change makes the trade-off a movement the learner watches, not a sentence.
The critique is shown on the same curve: 'Short Term' is struck, 'long term' is written, and the dot slides back.
Push arrows squeeze a dot that will not move while hatch lines pile up: NAIRU is seen before it is named.
Telling the topic as an idea that was believed and then challenged gives the lesson a story arc and a reason to listen.
'Schedule' is unpacked to the plain word suchi / list, which makes the whole term obvious.
Voices the learner's doubt (what difference does it make?) before giving three concrete benefits.
Names a common wrong belief (unscheduled = unregulated) and corrects it with the licence rule.
The root-cause hunt asks 'what does this depend on?' link by link, so the learner discovers what monetary policy must control before it is named.
The rich house owner who cannot buy a 25 lakh plane makes 'blocked money' unforgettable, and the voiced objection (sell the house) defines liquid money for free.
The CONTROL arms move to liquid money and the chain folds into the MONETARY POLICY badge exactly as the term is said.
'Let us break down this whole statement': the official one-line definition is unpacked phrase by phrase, each phrase becoming one step of the work.
A basket of mixed banknotes tied to the rupee note by a rope makes 'pegged to a basket' literal.
The weighted average is built in a table with assumed weights and real-looking rates, so the NEER is computed, not just defined.
'Think with a cool head' and 'I am sure you can work out the purpose yourself' make the learner infer before the answer.
Justifies the order of the next lessons (floating before LERMS) by prerequisite, not by date.
The rule is built first, so stagflation lands as a surprise twist: one red row breaking two green ones.
The word is split into STAG and FLATION, each half tied to its meaning: an easy memory hook.
The oil shock runs on the same resources -> economy -> GDP flow used at the start, so the cause sits where the learner already looks.
Running the scenario in reverse fills the second table row without a new explanation.
Analogy bridge: the known inflation question and its two indexes sit above the new currency question, so the learner expects two indexes before they are named.
The cause chain (many partners, many rates, cannot track each, need one index) gives the reason for the index before its method.
REER is taught as 'one small change' to the NEER table, so the second method costs only one new idea.
The 'but why?' question turns a claim into four reasons, and the 1-4 tab row keeps the learner oriented.
Everyday boasting stories and the newcomer's inner voice make market sentiment human.
After building the link, the contrast (short-term disconnect) stops the learner over-generalising.
The bond's cash-flow loop at a glance: investor's money up to the company, face value and coupon back on dotted arrows, both tagged fixed.
Fear then reassurance: the company runs away with your money, 'would you still invest?', then the spotlight of the rating agency on the issuer.
One bond passed along a chain of investors with the coupon arrow redrawn to the current holder: 'the coupon follows the bond' as a picture.
A column of return under each holder: the first reads coupon rate, the later ones 'more or less', then they are boxed and renamed bond yield.
The same chain is reused for primary and secondary market; only a coloured panel and the sidebar box move.
Seed in, harvest out: gross vs net with 10 and 100 before any formal word.
A machine's value curve falling to zero makes depreciation visible as a loss over time.
The formula is drawn as an arc from gross to net labelled '- depreciation' after two worked examples, so it reads as a summary, not a rule to memorise.
Two identical phones with YES and NO paths teach the boundary rule with one everyday object.
Starts from the learner's own loan and lifts it one level ('isi tarah banks bhi RBI se...'), so RBI's role is understood through a known act.
The policy effect is taught as a what-if with both directions on the same diagram (labels flip from decreased to increased), and LAF is named only after the effect is understood.
An explicit two-layer design: 'as a layman you now know enough; for UPSC we go deeper', so the learner gets the big idea before the mechanism.
The name 'repo' is unpacked from the deal itself ('we call it a loan but it is a sale and a purchase', hence repurchase agreement).
The learner's objection (why borrow for only 24 hours?) is voiced and answered with a recalled concept (CRR/SLR).
Reverse repo is the repo picture mirrored, with arrows reversed and 'repurchase' changed to 'resell'.
One curve, three slopes, three terms: each term is a shape the eye can check, and the definitions are built from one another (rate lower, then rate negative).
The same colour code is found again on real CPI data, so the made-up curve turns into a reading skill.
The counter-intuitive question (falling prices, falling demand?) is voiced as the learner's own doubt and answered through buyers' expectations.
Reflation is named only after the harm chain, so the term arrives as the answer to a felt problem.
A claim the learner just accepted (factor cost rises only with production) is shown, then stamped with a red cross: inflation opens the lesson.
Quantity stays 1 in every row while the laptop's price climbs 10K, 11K, 12.1K: GDP rises with nothing more made.
Inflation is a removable stripe inside the GDP block; it slides out, 'Nominal' is struck and 'REAL' written.
Dotted arcs hop back year by year along the line to a base year: 'how far back to remove inflation' is a picture.
The formula is built from the panels already on screen, then a balloon goes flat for 'hawa nikal deta hai'.
The sliding frame walks the curve one quarter at a time, so each term is a local pattern the eye can check for itself.
Recession is built from two contractions already seen, so the new term is defined only with old ones.
Depression stretches the same band, so the three 'falling' terms nest inside each other visually.
The crowd grows, the price is struck and rewritten, crosses fall under buyers who cannot pay and the packets go to the few who can: demand-pull seen before it is named.
The same scene with one packet removed shows exactly what changed; the 'but actually' turn then reframes it as bottleneck inflation.
A factory joined in front of the same template, with the voice stating demand and supply unchanged, isolates cost as the only cause.
Names who bears cost-push: buyers cut back on other things to pay the higher price.
The Monetarist frame sits under the whole Keynesian tree and loops up to both branches: one cause under two names.
One arrow per item, with height = size of the price rise, makes 'the overall price is an average of unequal moves' visible.
The 'but sometimes' contrast builds the new term out of the old one: average normal, a few items racing.
The what-if (only WPI watched) shows why the term was needed at all.
The learner's objection is voiced at the right moment (money parked in G-secs, a new customer walks in), so repo arrives as the answer to a felt problem.
One running example (NDTL 2000 crore) turns every percentage limit into crores on the picture, and the same numbers carry into MSF (20 + 20 = 40).
MSF enters only when the worked numbers hit the repo limit and demand doubles: the term is the answer to 'is there any option?'.
The repo channel fades away when the penalty rule is explained, leaving only the MSF loop, and RBI's personified scolding gives the reason for the penalty.
One anchor picture (investors -> invest -> India) is reused for every later idea, so each acronym is a branch of something already seen.
The learner's natural doubt ('what does the company gain?') is voiced and answered with a short cause chain (customs duty, cheap labour, policies).
Recaps both FDI routes on the tree before opening FPI, so the 10% line is fresh when FPI is defined as below it.
The rule (register with SEBI) is followed at once by its exception, shown as two investor kinds side by side with one feeding the other.
The rupee hangs from the dollar on a rod and rides the rising line: a peg made physical, then a ±1% chip shows the crawling peg as a small allowed band.
'Two things here' splits the system statement into two named sub-questions and answers them in that order.
A running character's car purchase turns the fixed rate into rupees and then into a money path through the bank, RBI and the reserve stack.
The same import is re-priced after devaluation (3.30 lakh to 4.76 lakh) and the rate cards line up as a history strip.
The recap is a visible cause chain, so the new question grows out of the learner's last lesson.
A household scene (5000 now, 1000 in an elder's time) builds the comparison first; 'basket' and 'base year' are then named as labels for parts of the story the learner already holds.
The supply chain with prices 10, 15, 20 and a what-if (the producer raises prices) gives a reason for indices at different points: a producer-side rise warns of consumer inflation.
The learner's likely confusion (food articles vs food products) is voiced and cleared with everyday examples: grown and edible, grown and not edible, processed.
One chair is followed through the whole calculation: quotes, price relatives, geometric mean, its index, its weight row, the weighted total.
Why the base year reads 100 is shown by reasoning, not stated: put current = base into the formula and everything cancels to 100.
Ownership as a region: the yellow nationalised zone grows over the timeline and every institution placed inside it reads as state-owned.
Thirty-three years of laws fold into one blue era band, then the band turns red for the crisis: one colour change tells the turn of the story.
The confusing 'Committee I' name is unpacked: same chairman, two committees, 1991 and 1998.
A dotted 'part of' arrow plugs the financial reforms into the bigger LPG package: nesting without a tree.
Clearing to the bare timeline gives a one-glance recap of 1947-1991 before the cliff-hanger question mark.
Need before name: goods in, money out; goods out, money in; so every dealing is in foreign currency, so a reserve is needed, and only then 'forex reserve'.
Summarise then name: a long list of dealings folds into one umbrella label for one year, which becomes the BoP document.
Double entry made concrete: a debit|credit board under every leaf, arrows to plus/minus, then frames adding heads into account totals, bottom-up.
The arc closes on the vault from minute one; the crisis is taught as a what-if about that vault running dry.

Banking is derived, not defined: a chain of problems (more demand, merchants short of cash, limited funds) leads step by step to loans at interest and deposits at a lower rate, and only then 'these agency houses are now working like banks', with a comparison to banks today.
Starts from what the learner already knows (banks around them and the RBI) and promises the story of why they exist.
The learner's objection (why would the Company compete with its own agents?) is voiced and answered by the shift of power by 1840.
The flashback is framed as a correction ('it is not that there were no banks before 1806') and drawn by extending the timeline to the left.
Each later institution arrives as the answer to a crisis (war panic, then the merger; depression, then the RBI Act and RBI), with a law-to-institution arc on the timeline.
Ends on an open question that the next video answers, a strong pull for a series.
Says openly that the data is hypothetical and cut to one month only to keep the calculation simple, which tells the learner what to ignore.
The contrast 'index against the base year, inflation against the previous year' sets up the whole effect in two short notes.
Surprise framing: the index rises by the same 10 every year, yet inflation falls; the term then names a puzzle the learner has already felt.
The role-play makes the problem felt before any term: the struck rate ladder and the rival-bank threat carry both 'rates were bargained' and 'competition pushes rates down'.
One bank and four identical people with different rate tags makes 'no standardisation' visible without reading.
The learner's obvious objection is put in RBI's mouth and answered by the banks, exposing that the 'minimum' was only an assumption.
The BPLR picture is reused for base rate; a gold ring on one bank and flipped arrows show that authority moved from RBI to each bank.
'Observe' cause chain: operating expenses differ by bank, so base rates must differ, yet each is a floor.
A red FAIL seal on the bank and 'bank fail hone ka matlab?' set the stakes before any term.
A spoken cause chain from one failed bank to all banks, to industry, to the economy, to the world, closed by a question the narrator answers himself.
The bus inner-pocket analogy makes 'keep capital aside' obvious to any learner (voice only).
Credit risk as a story: interest loop, more loans more risk, deposits flowing in, the loop crossed out, FAIL seal, then filed under 'credit risk' with an etymology unpack.
BIS as a hub with two-way arrows to central banks, and BCBS as a committee table with heads: institutions as small pictures.
The learner's objection ('no discount, so why buy?') is voiced, and the coupon arrives as its answer; the term coupon rate is named only after that, then 'zero coupon' is unpacked as 'no interest'.

One bond with a fixed 500 coupon passes through three owners at three prices, each price change has a story reason (needs liquidity, recession flight to safety, demand falls), and the yield is computed at each step before the term bond yield is defined.
The inverse rule is not stated as a formula first: the story's own numbers become points on the graph, so the rule is read off data the learner has already met.
A yes/no fork ('sold at a discount?') splits zero-coupon bond from bond in one picture.
A left road map keeps the learner's place in the capital-market tree, and its highlight moves to primary and secondary market as the narrator does.
The hook makes default risk personal (lost sleep after lending) and the same feeling returns as the payoff at 75 s, so the concept has an emotional before and after.
The risk disc slides from A to B just before the voice says 'risk transfer', so the conclusion line lands on a picture the learner has already seen.
The premium is explained in one sentence through the familiar insurance premium.
The slogan 'pehle security issue karo, phir paisa lo' is spoken as the same security-down / cash-up pair is copied to all five participants: one rule, one picture, used for the rest of the video.
The underworld analogy (a spoken word is trusted there, worthless here) makes 'security = written promise of amount, date, interest' memorable before the term.

Commercial bill taught as a short acted story (supplier, buyer, bank manager); the three flows close a loop on screen and the human benefit (both tensions end) and the bank's discount gain are spelled out.
Problem first: the government needs money for less than 91 days, 'what will it do?', and the cash management bill arrives as the cure.
Repo built from a what-if: the bank needs cash for only 25 days and does not want to sell for good, so the buy-back agreement is the natural answer.
The definition is a scene and a loop picture (a community starts a bank that serves the same community), so owner = customer is seen before the term is said.
The commercial bank is a mirror of the same picture: a small shareholder group owns it and a big public is served; goal 'profit' vs 'not profit'.

One complete worked example with numbers that balance: reserves as slices of the same money, rates compared with the commercial bank, a tally to +58 thousand, and what each member gains (better deposit rate, cheaper loan, dividend).
The structure is built bottom-up into empty tier slots with a fixed colour per bank type and counts like 'one per district', 'one per state'.
Registration is reached through the learner's own question ('which office do I go to?'), and each regulator enters only when a need appears (a bank needs a licence, so RBI).
A consolidation grid turns the regulators into a YES staircase and names dual and triple control, which sets up the next video's problem.
Everyday purchases flood the screen around one consumer and then snap into six labelled panels: classification is done by sorting real objects, not by a list.
The reference period is reasoned out loud before it is named: 7 days of food spending tells you enough, 7 days of rent tells you nothing, clothes need a year.
Segmentation is introduced as the answer to a problem (consumers differ by choice and purchasing power), then shown as baskets shrinking from a trolley to a tiny bag.
